questions.q: Upper GI bleeding is defined by a bleeding source located where?
ch: Confined to the duodenum distal to the ampulla of Vater
Proximal to the ligament of Treitz — esophagus, stomach, or duodenum
Distal to the ligament of Treitz in the jejunum and ileum
Anywhere in the colon, from the cecum through the rectum
Limited to the esophagus above the diaphragmatic hiatus
questions.exp: Upper GI bleeding arises from a source proximal to the ligament of Treitz — esophagus, stomach, and duodenum — and classically presents with hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, or melena.
why: The whole duodenum is included, and this definition would wrongly exclude the esophagus and stomach.
A source distal to the ligament of Treitz is by definition not an upper GI bleed.
Colonic bleeding presents as hematochezia and lies well distal to the ligament of Treitz.
The esophagus is only one of the three upper segments; the stomach and duodenum count as well.

questions.q: Which is the leading cause of upper GI bleeding?
ch: Esophagogastric varices from portal hypertension in cirrhosis
Peptic ulcer disease related to H. pylori or NSAIDs/aspirin
A Dieulafoy lesion eroding into a large submucosal artery
Erosive gastritis and esophagitis from acid mucosal injury
Mallory-Weiss tear following retching or forceful vomiting
questions.exp: Peptic ulcer disease — driven by H. pylori and NSAIDs/aspirin — is the leading cause of upper GI bleeding; the remaining causes include varices, Mallory-Weiss tears, erosive gastritis/esophagitis, malignancy, and Dieulafoy lesions.
why: Varices are the major variceal etiology but are less common overall than peptic ulcer disease.
A Dieulafoy lesion is listed among the other causes, not the leading one.
Erosive gastritis and esophagitis contribute but rank below peptic ulcer disease.
A Mallory-Weiss tear is a recognized cause but is far less common, and most stop spontaneously.

questions.q: Coffee-ground emesis in an upper GI bleed most directly reflects which process?
ch: Bile mixing with gastric contents from duodenogastric reflux
Swallowed blood from a nasopharyngeal rather than a luminal source
Brisk arterial bleeding with rapid transit through the stomach
Blood altered by gastric acid, implying a slower or stopped bleed
Blood retained in the colon long enough to be digested by bacteria
questions.exp: Coffee-ground emesis reflects blood altered by gastric acid, which implies a slower or already stopped upper bleed — unlike bright-red hematemesis, which signals active bleeding.
why: Bile-stained emesis is green-yellow and is not the altered blood of a coffee-ground appearance.
Swallowed blood can be vomited, but the coffee-ground appearance itself reflects acid alteration, not the origin.
Brisk bleeding gives bright-red hematemesis, or even hematochezia, because the blood has no time to be altered by acid.
Coffee-ground material is vomited from the stomach; colonic retention is not what alters it.

questions.q: A patient arrives with active hematemesis. Which nursing action takes priority?
ch: Position the patient flat and supine to maximize cerebral perfusion pressure
Send a stool specimen for occult blood before other interventions
Give an oral proton pump inhibitor and start clear liquids as tolerated
Arrange upper endoscopy immediately, before any resuscitation is started
Establish two large-bore IVs (16-18 gauge), apply oxygen, and prepare for volume resuscitation
questions.exp: The priority is ABCs: two large-bore IVs (16-18 gauge), oxygen, and preparation for volume resuscitation before anything else — resuscitate before you investigate.
why: Positioning should protect the airway against aspiration of hematemesis, with suction ready.
Overt hematemesis already establishes the bleed; occult blood testing only delays resuscitation.
The patient is kept NPO for endoscopy, and the proton pump inhibitor is given intravenously.
EGD is the gold standard but follows stabilization — a stable patient tolerates endoscopy far better.

questions.q: A BUN:creatinine ratio above 30:1 in a bleeding patient points to what?
ch: A falsely elevated hemoglobin from hemoconcentration
Active hemolysis rather than luminal blood loss
An upper source — digested blood as a nitrogen load plus a prerenal state
A lower GI source distal to the ligament of Treitz
Intrinsic renal failure from acute tubular necrosis
questions.exp: Blood is a cathartic and a nitrogen load, so digested blood plus a prerenal state elevates the BUN; a BUN:creatinine ratio above 30:1 is a useful bedside clue pointing to an upper source over a lower one.
why: Hemoglobin may be falsely normal early because whole blood is lost proportionally, but that is unrelated to the BUN.
The nitrogen load here comes from blood digested in the gut lumen, not from intravascular hemolysis.
A lower source does not deliver the same nitrogen load to be absorbed and does not raise the ratio this way.
Intrinsic renal failure typically lowers the ratio rather than driving it above 30:1.

questions.q: Which transfusion strategy is recommended for a hemodynamically stable patient with an acute upper GI bleed?
ch: A restrictive threshold, transfusing to a hemoglobin target of 7-8 g/dL
Withhold all blood products until endoscopy identifies the source
Transfuse only once the hemoglobin has fallen below 5 g/dL
A liberal threshold, transfusing to keep hemoglobin above 10 g/dL
Fresh frozen plasma routinely in place of packed RBC transfusion
questions.exp: A restrictive transfusion threshold (Hgb 7 g/dL, target 7-8) is used in stable patients; liberal transfusion raises portal pressure and disrupts clot, increasing rebleeding and mortality (Villanueva, NEJM 2013).
why: Resuscitation with crystalloid and packed RBCs precedes endoscopy rather than waiting on it.
That threshold is far below the recommended 7 g/dL and would leave the patient dangerously anemic.
Liberal transfusion increases rebleeding and mortality and is exactly what the restrictive strategy avoids.
Packed RBCs restore oxygen delivery; PCC is preferred over FFP for warfarin reversal, and plasma is not a routine substitute.

questions.q: A Glasgow-Blatchford Score of 0-1 identifies which kind of patient?
ch: A patient with the highest predicted rebleeding and mortality risk
A patient requiring prophylactic intubation before upper endoscopy
A very-low-risk patient potentially safe for outpatient management
A patient needing immediate balloon tamponade of bleeding varices
A patient with a Forrest Ia spurting ulcer requiring urgent therapy
questions.exp: The Glasgow-Blatchford Score identifies low-risk patients who may avoid admission; a score of 0-1 flags a very-low-risk patient potentially safe for outpatient management.
why: That is what the Rockall score predicts, and a Glasgow-Blatchford of 0-1 means the lowest risk, not the highest.
Prophylactic intubation is considered for ongoing hematemesis with altered mental status, a red flag rather than a low score.
Balloon tamponade is reserved for refractory variceal bleeding, the opposite end of the risk spectrum.
The Forrest classification grades endoscopic stigmata after scoping; Forrest Ia is a high-risk lesion, not a low score.

questions.q: A cirrhotic patient with hematemesis is started on octreotide before endoscopy. Which added therapy independently reduces mortality?
ch: Fresh frozen plasma to fully normalize the INR
Liberal transfusion to a hemoglobin above 10 g/dL
High-dose oral beta-blocker during the acute bleed
Tranexamic acid as an antifibrinolytic adjunct
Prophylactic ceftriaxone, given to every cirrhotic with a GI bleed
questions.exp: Antibiotic prophylaxis with ceftriaxone is standard of care for every cirrhotic with a GI bleed and is given even without overt infection — it independently reduces infection, rebleeding, and mortality, making it as important as octreotide.
why: Coagulopathy should not be over-corrected in cirrhosis, and PCC is preferred over FFP when reversal is needed.
Liberal transfusion raises portal pressure and worsens variceal rebleeding and mortality.
A nonselective beta-blocker is for secondary prevention after recovery, not during the acute bleed.
Tranexamic acid is not recommended: HALT-IT showed no mortality benefit and more venous thromboembolism and seizures.

questions.q: Why is tranexamic acid no longer recommended in acute GI bleeding?
ch: It raises portal pressure and provokes variceal rebleeding
It obscures endoscopic visualization of the gastric mucosa
It prolongs the QT interval the way intravenous erythromycin does
The HALT-IT trial showed no mortality benefit and more thromboembolism and seizures
It reverses the effect of proton pump inhibitors on gastric pH
questions.exp: Tranexamic acid was historically considered an antifibrinolytic adjunct, but the HALT-IT trial showed no mortality benefit and increased venous thromboembolism and seizures, so it is not recommended.
why: Raising portal pressure and disrupting clot is the problem with liberal transfusion, not with tranexamic acid.
Visualization is addressed by giving intravenous erythromycin as a prokinetic to clear gastric blood.
QT prolongation is the caution attached to erythromycin, not the reason tranexamic acid was abandoned.
Tranexamic acid has no effect on gastric pH; the PPI raises pH to stabilize clot independently.

questions.q: Esophageal variceal bleeding continues despite octreotide and band ligation. What is the appropriate escalation?
ch: Balloon tamponade as a bridge, with TIPS as definitive therapy
Repeat a high-dose proton pump inhibitor infusion and observe
Epinephrine injection with thermal coagulation of the varices
Start tranexamic acid to correct an antifibrinolytic deficit
Observation with serial hemoglobin measurement every six hours
questions.exp: For refractory variceal bleeding, escalate to balloon tamponade as a bridge and TIPS as definitive therapy; angiographic embolization or surgery is the parallel escalation for uncontrolled ulcer bleeding.
why: High-dose PPI targets non-variceal peptic ulcer bleeding and does nothing for portal pressure.
Epinephrine plus a second modality is the endoscopic therapy for high-risk ulcers; varices are treated with band ligation.
Tranexamic acid is not recommended in GI bleeding after HALT-IT showed harm without benefit.
Ongoing bleeding is a red flag for hemodynamic collapse; observation is not an escalation.

questions.q: Most gallstones in cholelithiasis are composed of what?
ch: Uric acid stones related to hyperuricemia and gout
Protein and bile salt plugs formed purely from bile stasis
Cholesterol stones, which make up roughly 75% of gallstones
Pigment stones, seen with hemolysis, cirrhosis, or infection
Calcium oxalate crystals, as in renal stone disease
questions.exp: Cholelithiasis means gallstones in the gallbladder, and roughly 75% of them are cholesterol stones; the rest are pigment stones associated with hemolysis, cirrhosis, or infection.
why: Uric acid stones are a renal stone type; gallstones are classified as cholesterol or pigment.
Bile stasis matters most in acalculous disease, where by definition there are no stones at all.
Pigment stones make up the minority, forming the remainder after cholesterol stones.
Calcium oxalate is a urinary stone composition and is not the makeup of gallstones.

questions.q: Acute calculous cholecystitis results most directly from which event?
ch: A stone lodged in the common bile duct with rising bilirubin
Bile stasis and ischemia in a fasting, critically ill patient
Ascending bacterial infection of the intrahepatic bile ducts
A stone impacted in the cystic duct, causing wall edema and distension
A stone eroding through the wall into the adjacent small bowel
questions.exp: Acute cholecystitis is usually caused by a stone impacted in the cystic duct (calculous, about 90%), producing wall edema, gallbladder distension, mucosal ischemia, and secondary infection.
why: A stone in the common bile duct is choledocholithiasis, suggested by markedly high bilirubin and ALP or a dilated duct.
That mechanism describes acalculous cholecystitis, which occurs without stones.
Ascending infection of the ducts is cholangitis; infection in cholecystitis is secondary to the obstruction.
A stone eroding into the gut causes gallstone ileus, a late complication rather than the initiating event.

questions.q: The classic “5 F's” mnemonic for cholelithiasis risk stands for which set of factors?
ch: Fasting, Fistula, Fibrosis, Failure, Fracture
Female, Fat, Forty, Fertile, Fair
Family history, Fluid overload, Fever, Fatigue, Fainting
Fat intolerance, Fetor, Fissure, Fibroma, Frequency
Fever, Fatigue, Flatulence, Fullness, Flushing
questions.exp: The 5 F's — Female, Fat, Forty, Fertile, Fair — is the classic cholelithiasis risk mnemonic; rapid weight loss, pregnancy, and estrogen therapy also raise risk.
why: Fasting does predispose to acalculous disease, but this is not the classic risk mnemonic.
These items are not the five factors in the mnemonic taught for gallstone risk.
Fat intolerance is a symptom of biliary disease, and the rest are unrelated to gallstone risk.
These are symptoms rather than the demographic risk factors the mnemonic captures.

questions.q: Which examination finding is described as Murphy’s sign?
ch: Pain on passive extension of the right hip with the knee flexed
Flank ecchymosis appearing two to three days after symptom onset
A palpable, nontender gallbladder in a jaundiced patient
Rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant at McBurney’s point
Inspiratory arrest on deep RUQ palpation, sensitive for acute cholecystitis
questions.exp: Murphy's sign is inspiratory arrest on deep RUQ palpation and is sensitive for acute cholecystitis; the same finding seen during ultrasound is a sonographic Murphy's sign, and pain may radiate to the right scapula or shoulder.
why: That is a psoas sign; biliary pain instead radiates to the right scapula or shoulder.
Flank ecchymosis points to retroperitoneal hemorrhage, not to cystic duct obstruction.
A palpable nontender gallbladder with jaundice is Courvoisier's sign, which points to malignant obstruction rather than stones.
Right lower quadrant rebound suggests appendicitis, not gallbladder inflammation.

questions.q: RUQ ultrasound is first-line for suspected acute cholecystitis. Which combination of findings confirms it?
ch: A dilated common bile duct containing a filling defect on MRCP
Diffuse calcification of the gallbladder wall without any stones
Stones, wall thickening over 3 mm, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's sign
Nonvisualization of the gallbladder after radiotracer administration
Pneumobilia with small-bowel obstruction on plain radiography
questions.exp: RUQ ultrasound is first-line and confirmatory: it shows stones, gallbladder wall thickening over 3 mm, pericholecystic fluid, and a sonographic Murphy's sign.
why: A dilated duct with a stone indicates choledocholithiasis rather than gallbladder inflammation.
Wall calcification is a porcelain gallbladder, which raises cancer risk but is not acute inflammation.
Nonvisualization is the HIDA scan finding, used when the ultrasound is equivocal.
Air in the biliary tree with obstruction describes gallstone ileus, a separate complication.

questions.q: When RUQ ultrasound is equivocal, which study is the most specific for acute cholecystitis?
ch: Repeat ultrasound in 24 hours after a fatty meal challenge
Abdominal plain films looking for a porcelain gallbladder
Serum lipase to exclude a coexisting gallstone pancreatitis
ERCP to visualize and clear the common bile duct
HIDA scan — nonvisualization of the gallbladder confirms cystic duct obstruction
questions.exp: The HIDA scan (cholescintigraphy) is the most specific test: nonvisualization of the gallbladder confirms cystic duct obstruction when the ultrasound is equivocal.
why: Repeating a nondiagnostic ultrasound delays care when a more specific test is available.
Plain films may show a porcelain gallbladder or pneumobilia but cannot confirm acute cholecystitis.
Lipase evaluates the pancreas and says nothing about cystic duct obstruction.
ERCP is reserved for suspected choledocholithiasis or cholangitis, not for confirming gallbladder inflammation.

questions.q: A patient has RUQ pain, fever, and jaundice together. Which diagnosis does this triad indicate?
ch: Acalculous cholecystitis in a critically ill patient
Cholangitis — Charcot's triad, which is not cholecystitis
Gallstone ileus with pneumobilia and bowel obstruction
Acute cholecystitis with a positive Murphy’s sign
Biliary colic triggered by a recent fatty meal
questions.exp: Charcot's triad — RUQ pain, fever, and jaundice — indicates ascending cholangitis; adding hypotension and altered mental status makes Reynolds' pentad and signals septic shock requiring urgent biliary decompression by ERCP.
why: Acalculous disease is defined by the absence of stones in a critically ill patient, not by this triad.
Gallstone ileus presents with small-bowel obstruction and air in the biliary tree, not with jaundice and fever.
Cholecystitis gives persistent RUQ pain and fever, but jaundice is not part of its classic picture.
Biliary colic is intermittent pain that resolves, without fever or leukocytosis.

questions.q: A stable patient with mild acute cholecystitis has been resuscitated with IV fluids and started on antibiotics. What is the definitive management?
ch: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ideally within 72 hours
Ursodeoxycholic acid to dissolve the stones over several months
Percutaneous cholecystostomy as the definitive procedure
Delayed cholecystectomy after six weeks of oral antibiotics
ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction from the duct
questions.exp: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the definitive treatment, and early surgery within 72 hours lowers morbidity and shortens hospital stay compared with delayed surgery.
why: Ursodeoxycholic acid is slow, of low efficacy, and reserved for nonsurgical candidates — it is not for acute cholecystitis.
Cholecystostomy is the option for a poor surgical candidate, and it is a bridge rather than definitive therapy.
Delaying surgery increases morbidity compared with operating within 72 hours.
ERCP addresses stones in the common bile duct, which is a different problem from an inflamed gallbladder.

questions.q: A critically ill post-op patient on TPN develops fever and RUQ pain, and ultrasound shows no stones. What is the likely diagnosis?
ch: Acalculous cholecystitis from bile stasis and ischemia
Biliary colic from a stone that has already passed
Porcelain gallbladder with malignant transformation
Mirizzi syndrome from a stone compressing the hepatic duct
Gallstone ileus from a stone eroding into the small bowel
questions.exp: Acalculous cholecystitis occurs without stones in critically ill, fasting, TPN, or post-op patients from bile stasis and ischemia; it carries higher morbidity, so keep a low threshold for HIDA and percutaneous drainage.
why: Biliary colic is intermittent pain that resolves and does not produce fever in a critically ill patient.
A porcelain gallbladder is a chronic calcified wall raising cancer risk, not an acute febrile illness.
Mirizzi syndrome requires a stone, and the ultrasound here shows none.
Gallstone ileus needs a stone and presents with small-bowel obstruction and pneumobilia.

questions.q: A patient admitted with acute cholecystitis develops markedly rising bilirubin and ALP with a dilated common bile duct. What does this suggest?
ch: Post-cholecystectomy syndrome from retained insufflated gas
Simple biliary colic that will resolve without intervention
Emphysematous cholecystitis with crepitus over the wall
Choledocholithiasis — obtain MRCP or ERCP for duct stones
Courvoisier's sign of malignant biliary obstruction
questions.exp: Markedly elevated bilirubin and ALP with a dilated common bile duct is the red flag for choledocholithiasis; the next step is MRCP or ERCP to find and clear the duct stone.
why: This patient has not had surgery, and insufflated CO2 causes referred shoulder pain rather than duct dilation.
Biliary colic is transient pain without fever, leukocytosis, or a rising bilirubin and dilated duct.
Emphysematous cholecystitis is signaled by crepitus and peritoneal signs, not by an obstructive lab pattern.
Courvoisier's sign is a palpable nontender gallbladder with jaundice and points away from stones.
